# Method {#sec-method}

## The objective is paper 2b's and paper 3's

The likelihood does not change in this paper. Each runner $j$ in race $r$
receives a score $z_{rj}$, and the probability of the observed finishing
order down to depth $k$ is the Plackett–Luce form
[@plackett1975; @luce1959] that paper 2b's exploded conditional logit fits
and paper 3's custom objective optimises:

$$
\Pr(\text{top-}k \text{ order}) \;=\; \prod_{s=1}^{S}
\frac{\exp(z_{r,(s)})}{\sum_{j \in R_{r,s}} \exp(z_{rj})},
\qquad S = \min(k,\, J_r - 1),
$$

where $(s)$ is the horse that finished $s$-th and $R_{r,s}$ is the set still
unplaced at stage $s$. Depth $k = 3$ throughout, as in papers 2b and 3. At
$k = 1$ this is McFadden's conditional logit [@mcfadden1974], which is
paper 1's model.

What changes across the series is only the function producing $z$: a linear
predictor in papers 1, 2a and 2b, a gradient-boosted tree ensemble in paper
3, and a neural scorer here. The loss is implemented directly in `{torch}`
and verified against paper 3's analytic gradient, so this paper descends the
same surface paper 3 did; @sec-appx-a gives the verification.

Weights are shared across horses. The scorer maps one runner's features to
one number, and runners are coupled only through the per-race denominator.

## A ladder, one change at a rung

The paper is built as a ladder. Each rung changes exactly one thing about
how a horse's history reaches the scorer and is compared with the rung
below it, so that a difference in ranking can be attributed to that change
and not to a bundle of them.

| rung | the one change | comparator |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | linear scorer → multi-layer perceptron, identical features | paper 2b's linear predictor |
| 2 | three strike rates → embeddings for trainer, jockey and sire | rung 1 |
| 3 | eight history summaries → sequence encoder | rung 1 |

The difference between two models is stated and asserted in code before
either is fitted, rather than left to prose.

Two further rungs were specified and not run. Adding embeddings
**alongside** the strike rates rather than in place of them would only test
whether they help where the strike rate is already most reliable, since an
embedding can only be learned for entities that appear often enough in the
fitting data. A Deep Sets encoder over today's field — a summary of the
other runners rather than of the horse's own past — would be fitted at race
grain: `r p5_comma(n_train_races)` races against `r p5_comma(n_train_rows)`
runner-rows, an order of magnitude less data than every other rung, and a
new architecture at the same time.

## Selection, and what it was allowed to see

Nine configurations per model, declared in full before any of them was
scored. Selection saw validation Plackett–Luce loss and nothing else: never
a ranking metric, never a betting return, never a test row.

In every rung the best epoch arrived within about three passes over the
training data, and the validation loss rose steadily afterwards. Early
stopping therefore does real work, and it is done the same way for every
model — the parameters kept are those from the best validation epoch.

## The two models that reach the test split

The hand-built model scores 26 features. The encoder model scores 18 of
those 26 — the eight history summaries of @sec-data are the ones removed —
plus `career_runs_prior` and the sequence encoder's output. The downstream
scorer, the objective, the races, the validation slice and the seed are
identical.

Both are refitted on the **full** training split — the validation slice
folded back in — at the configuration the slice selected, then score the
test split once. Both train for the same number of epochs, the epoch each
selected on validation, and there is no per-epoch evaluation at that stage:
with no held-out set left, scoring the test split each epoch would put it
inside the selection loop.

One consequence is worth stating plainly. The full training split is about
43% larger than the fitting partition used for selection, so an epoch is 43%
more gradient steps than it was during selection. Both models take that
change identically, so the contrast between them is unaffected by it.
